source: OpenLearn (Open University) Jury decision making: what's the story?
finding: The page states the three standard critiques of the story model. (1) Group deliberation: a jury is more than the sum of its members, and the theory is thin on it. (2) Formalism: the model assumes a logical, rule-bound process and struggles with extra-legal factors such as juror values. (3) Why story form matters: it is not clear what the story form adds.
numbers: Only number in the page: a jury can flip from 11-1 for conviction to 12-0 for acquittal during debate. Cites Hastie et al. 1983, Devine et al. 2001, Diamond & Rose 2018.
limits: Popular-level summary, not a primary critique. The 11-1 to 12-0 flip is an illustration, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Scoring caution: the story model describes one mind building one account. Do not treat the output of one sample as a group verdict; an agent that deliberates needs its own mechanism for changing its mind.

source: OpenLearn (Open University) Jury decision making: what's the story?
finding: Third critique in detail: the same cognitive model could be written as stories, computer code, a connectionist net or neural activity, so the story form itself has no demonstrated causal role. Story form is claimed to help individual cognition (familiar characters, desires, intentions) but this is asserted, not tested against other formats.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Pennington & Hastie 1991 as the source of the claim.
quote: there seems to be a chapter missing from the story
limits: Argument by a commentator; no experiment compares story format with an equally coherent non-story format.
agent_relevance: For our agent: a causal chain with goals may be the useful part, not the prose form. Score the structure (causal links, completeness, uniqueness), not narrative style.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror
finding: Interview study (Pennington 1981; Pennington & Hastie 1986): 26 jury-pool volunteers watched a filmed murder trial (Commonwealth v. Johnson) and talked aloud. A 16-juror subsample was analysed. Their evidence summaries had story form, not argument form, and jurors with different verdicts built different stories.
numbers: N=26 volunteers, 16 analysed. Verdicts of the 16: 5 first-degree murder, 4 second-degree, 4 manslaughter, 3 not guilty. 85% of events in protocols were causally linked. Only 55% of protocol references were to events in testimony; 45% were inferred events. Character inferences were 5.4% of story content. Verdict stories were the events and links shared by 80% of a verdict group.
limits: The authors themselves say the interview method may have created a demand for stories as justification. Single case, small N, subsample chosen to get a spread of verdicts.
agent_relevance: Nearly half of the story content is inferred, not given. An agent building a story will fill gaps; each filled gap needs a flag and a check (guardrail G3).

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror
finding: Verdict category learning did not explain verdict choice. Memory for verdict-element relations, content of verdict understanding, and beyond-reasonable-doubt thresholds did not differ by verdict group. Verdict covaried with story structure only.
numbers: No significant differences by verdict group on verdict-element memory (Pennington & Hastie 1986) or on ratings of reasonable-doubt threshold and presumption of innocence (Hastie et al. 1983, same pool and trial).
limits: Null results, sample sizes not restated in the chapter. Supports story as the driver but does not rule out that story and verdict were chosen together.
agent_relevance: Separate the two steps in the scaffold: build the account, then classify it against the rule. Most variance sits in the first step.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror
finding: Recognition-memory study (Pennington & Hastie 1988): mock jurors falsely recognised inferred story sentences that fit their own verdict, and rated evidence importance by its causal role in their verdict story. Offered as proof that stories form spontaneously, not only when asked in an interview.
numbers: 119-sentence written version of the case; old targets and new lures taken from each verdict story. Exact hit and false-alarm rates are not given in the chapter.
limits: Chapter admits this still does not show the story causes the verdict; it could be a post hoc justification.
agent_relevance: A story-consistent false memory is the risk: the agent should re-check inferred items against source text before using them as evidence.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror
finding: Order-of-evidence experiment (third study). Same content, presented in story order or witness order, changed verdicts. Used as the causal test that story ease drives the decision.
numbers: 130 college mock jurors, 100 evidence statements (50 prosecution, 50 defense), forced choice murder vs not guilty. Percent guilty by prosecution/defense order: story/story 59%, story/witness 78%, witness/story 31%, witness/witness 63%. Row means: prosecution story order 69%, witness order 47%. Column means: defense story order 45%, witness order 70%. Jurors who heard both sides in story order were most confident.
limits: Authors: lab study stripped of opening and closing statements, so it does not estimate size of order effects in real trials. Replication cited: Smith 1988 (story vs legal-issue order). Table layout in the scanned text is garbled; cell assignment follows the text (78 and 31 are stated in words).
agent_relevance: Format of the input (chronological and causal vs by-witness) moves the outcome by up to 47 points. Present evidence to the agent in a reorderable form and test both orders; if the answer flips with order, flag low confidence.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror
finding: Fourth study (Pennington & Hastie 1992): story order vs legal-issue order, two cases (evidence favouring guilt or innocence). Story order raised story clustering in free recall and shifted verdicts and confidence in the expected direction, with no change in total recall, so order was not just a memorability effect.
numbers: 414 college students, written materials, cases from Devine & Ostrom (1985). Clustering measured with the adjusted ratio of clustering (ARC). Total amount recalled equal across conditions.
limits: Verdict percentages per cell are not given in the chapter. Student sample, written trial, no deliberation.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as a06, with a control for memory load: organisation, not amount of information, changed the judgment.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror
finding: Fifth and sixth studies (Pennington & Hastie 1992): adding story-completing supplements pushed guilt judgments toward the completed story. Judgments made once at the end (global) were more story-driven than judgments made after each item. Item-by-item ratings fit an anchor-and-adjust model; global ratings fit a story-weighted model; Bayesian aggregation fit neither.
numbers: Bayesian aggregates of local ratings were about 10 times stronger than global ratings and about 15 times stronger than item-by-item ratings (subjects were very conservative). Global assessments were about 1.5 times stronger than final item-by-item judgments. Anchor-and-adjust model weights: current judgment .45, new block .55.
limits: Model comparison on student ratings of two stimulus cases; goodness-of-fit statistics not restated in the chapter.
agent_relevance: Evidence order and the point of judgment change the result. Judge once, after all evidence, from a built account; do not update a running score item by item (supports our one-judgment-after-build design).

source: Hastie (2008) What's the story? Explanations and narratives in civil jury decisions, ch. 1 in Diamond & Bornstein (eds.), Civil Juries
finding: Hastie summarises what was established and extends to civil cases. In one-sided criminal cases jurors build one story, and confidence tracks fit of that story to the verdict. A weak defense story can make the prosecution story stronger than no defense story at all (McKenzie, Lee & Chen 2002). Priming the story in the opening statement raises story-consistent verdicts.
numbers: No new numbers in this paragraph. Cites Pennington & Hastie 1986, 1988, 1992; McKenzie et al. 2002.
limits: Secondary retelling by the theory's author; McKenzie et al. not opened.
agent_relevance: A weak counter-story can backfire. If the agent generates a rival story, it must be real and checked; a flimsy rival raises confidence in the favourite.

source: Hastie (2008) What's the story? Explanations and narratives in civil jury decisions, ch. 1 in Diamond & Bornstein (eds.), Civil Juries
finding: Civil punitive-damages think-aloud study (Hastie, Schkade & Payne 1998; plus 20 college students). Most mock jurors built a chronological causal narrative first. They then judged causation, then some legal elements. Few covered all the elements the judge listed.
numbers: Four cases, Denver-area citizens. In the student sample (N=20): 15 (75%) relied mainly on narrative summaries, 3 (15%) on legal elements, 2 (10%) neither. Coder agreement over 90%. 12 (60%) explicitly considered a causation issue; 17 (84%) discussed one conduct element; 11 (55%) another; 6 (30%) considered malice or reasonableness.
limits: N=20 students; percentages are counts out of 20. Author states most jurors fell short of the fully conscientious model.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for the formalism critique from inside the theory: people use a story and cover the legal checklist only partly. Our agent should have code check every required element, not trust the story to cover them.

source: Rossner (2019) Storytelling Rituals in Jury Deliberations, Oñati Socio-Legal Series 9(5)
finding: Qualitative video analysis of one 12-person mock jury deliberation (Australian JIVE project). Names the gap in the story model: it explains one juror's story but not how many private stories become a shared master narrative. In the case, a juror's alternative story was first rejected, then accepted for testing after rapport built through humour and shared focus.
numbers: One jury of 12, one facilitated deliberation; no verdict counts.
quote: What is missing from this account is an explanation of the role of group-level deliberation dynamics.
limits: Author's own limits: a facilitator was present, no unanimous verdict was required, and mock jurors were used. Claims are matched to real-jury work (Maynard & Manzo 1993, Conley & Conley 2009, Gibson 2016).
agent_relevance: The same story can be refused or heard depending on how it is introduced. For multi-agent designs: a minority account needs a turn structure that makes it testable, not just stated.

source: Rossner (2019) Storytelling Rituals in Jury Deliberations
finding: Deliberation is described as two or more competing stories being compared for best fit, with credibility of expert witnesses used as the test (an animated bomb-path expert for the prosecution vs a cardboard-box alternative from the defense). Story testing is social work, not only cognitive work.
numbers: Transcript excerpts only; no quantitative data.
limits: Single case, interpretive coding, no replication.
agent_relevance: Fit comparison of rival accounts matches our competing-hypothesis state, but humans do it through argument. Agent debate must be constructed so each side answers the other's specific claims.

source: Vlex abstract: Simon, 'Thin empirics' (commentary on Allen & Pardo, relative plausibility)
finding: A legal-psychology critique of using the story model to ground a general theory of fact-finding. Simon calls the story model brilliant but says it is too narrow a base, and that the target article offers no unit of analysis, no testable hypotheses and no data.
numbers: No numbers in the opened excerpt (abstract and opening only).
quote: the Story Model provides too narrow a foundation to sustain a general model of legal fact-finding
limits: Only an excerpt was read, not the full commentary. Year and venue not confirmed from the page.
agent_relevance: Do not generalise from a handful of mock-trial studies to all fact-finding. Treat story-based scoring as a tested heuristic for crime-type narrative cases, not a universal rule.

source: Cohen & Berryessa (2026) The Role of the Dissenting Voter on Jury Deliberation Online: A Pilot Study, Behavioral Sciences 16(10):1960
finding: Virtual mock juries with a trained confederate who dissented. Deliberation moved all initial not-guilty voters to guilty, not toward the dissenter. Qualitative coding found substantive discussion of competing readings of the evidence.
numbers: 35 participants, 7 six-person Zoom juries. 34 with paired data: 28 (82.4%) guilty and 6 (17.6%) not guilty before; all 34 guilty after. Exact McNemar p = 0.031. Confederate dissent in 6 juries, organic dissent in 1. Longest deliberation 16 minutes.
limits: Pilot; 7 juries so votes are nested and the test is only descriptive; short sessions; confederate protocol.
agent_relevance: Deliberation can wash out the minority, the opposite of the 11-1 to 12-0 picture. Majority pressure, not argument quality, may decide; a multi-agent vote needs guarding against this.

source: Cohen & Berryessa (2026) The Role of the Dissenting Voter on Jury Deliberation Online
finding: The paper restates the stock argument that deliberation can reflect real persuasion or mere accommodation to the majority, and that the two are hard to tell apart. Asch-type conformity falls when one dissenter breaks unanimity.
numbers: No new numbers; cites Asch 1951/1956, Devine et al. 2001, Davenport & Winet 2022.
limits: Introduction text, citing others.
agent_relevance: A change of answer is not evidence of better reasoning. Log why an answer changed (new evidence vs social pull) before counting a revision as good.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents: Evaluating Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making Through Cinematic Jury Deliberation, arXiv 2605.01986
finding: Twelve LLM jurors began 11 guilty to 1 not guilty (the classic 11-1 swing setup). Almost none moved. 17 of 18 runs ended in a hung jury. The film's minority-to-majority persuasion almost never occurred.
numbers: GPT-4o and Llama-4-Scout, 3 conditions, N=3 per cell, 18 runs, temperature 0.9, up to 150 turns, hung jury called after 3 vote rounds with no change. GPT-4o: 9 of 9 hung. Llama: 8 hung, 1 not guilty (64 turns, 6 vote changes, no-initial-vote condition).
limits: Exploratory; N=3 per cell; no significance tests; persona prompts with assigned votes; one film case; one orchestration framework (AutoGen SelectorGroupChat).
agent_relevance: LLM groups anchor on the starting position, so panel deliberation adds little by itself. Our design uses independent attempts plus code checks, not chat between copies.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents
finding: Alignment-heavy GPT-4o stayed flat; Llama-4-Scout responded to an open-minded instruction. The paper attributes this to RLHF intensity, a hypothesis not tested directly.
numbers: Mean vote changes per run, GPT-4o: 1.0 baseline, 0.7 no initial vote, 1.0 open-minded. Llama-4-Scout: 2.0, 3.3, 6.0 (runs 5, 5, 8). Mean Llama turns in open-minded condition 72.
limits: Two models only, so RLHF is confounded with architecture, size and persona handling. N=3.
agent_relevance: A prompt line saying 'be open-minded' is not a reliable lever. Consistent with our guardrail that doubt must be triggered by a code-checked signal, not requested in prose (G1).

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents
finding: Qualitative gap: LLM jurors cite the same evidence as the film's jurors and acknowledge counter-arguments but do not update on them. No emotional rupture, no coalition formation, and agents speak in parallel monologues with rare cross-reference.
numbers: All 18 runs cited the same evidence items (knife, old man, woman across the street, train timing, threat). No agent deviated from its assigned start vote at the first vote check.
limits: Author's interpretation of transcripts; no coded inter-rater scores given in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Agents given a fixed story or role resist change. Role-prompted voters in our scaffold would not give independent evidence (G4).

source: Wu (2026) When Does Defendant Statement Matter? A Study of Bias and Persuasion in LLM-Simulated Jurors (JuryBench), arXiv 2609.09887
finding: Large LLM jury simulation, but at individual-juror level with no deliberation. Findings echo human results: emotional appeals can backfire, background match between juror and defendant is a strong factor, and juror ideology shifts severity.
numbers: 20 frontier LLMs, about 432K decisions and rationales, controversial U.S. criminal cases, defendant statements varied, jurors with ideology scores from -5 to +5. Shares such as 'around 60%' and 'around 70%' of LLMs are reported for specific effects; exact per-model effects not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract, introduction and some results text were read. No group deliberation, so it does not address the main critique.
agent_relevance: LLM jury studies mostly test the single-juror step. The deliberation gap in the critique is untested in the larger AI literature, so do not score our agent on group-level claims from these.

source: Misinformation presented during jury deliberation and juror memory and decision-making (Frontiers, 2024)
finding: Two experiments in which participants read a deliberation transcript with planted misinformation from simulated jurors. Misinformation was often misattributed to trial evidence, and pro-defense misinformation skewed decisions in Study 2. A judicial instruction warning of misinformation had no effect.
numbers: Study 1 N=275 (12-minute e-deliberation; pro-prosecution, pro-defense or contradictory). Study 2 N=339. In the instruction condition only 11 participants (6.5%) could report the warning when asked to paraphrase it. Bayes factors reported with frequentist tests.
limits: Participants read a transcript of simulated jurors, so no live interaction. Sexual-assault case; rape-myth belief moderated results.
agent_relevance: What others say in deliberation can overwrite what was in the source. Applied to agents: peer text must be tagged and checked against the original evidence before it is believed.

source: The effect of verdict system on juror decisions: a quantitative meta-analysis (2025)
finding: Verdict options change individual juror decisions. With three verdicts (Scottish: guilty, not guilty, not proven) conviction odds were about 40% lower than with two verdicts, before any deliberation. Bears on the 'formal process' critique: the decision depends on the category set, not only on the story.
numbers: 10 mock trials, 1778 jurors, pooled OR = 0.625, 95% CI [0.51, 0.77]. Heterogeneity Cochran's Q(9) = 12.28, p = .198, I2 = 22.2%. Funnel asymmetry test tau = .02, p = 1.0. The only civil trial was the outlier.
limits: Only pre-deliberation individual verdicts used and treated as independent; mock trials with varied participant sources (some not drawn from the electoral roll).
agent_relevance: The same story can lead to different outputs under different answer menus. Fix the answer set before scoring and report it with the result.

source: Hastie, Penrod & Pennington (1983) Inside the Jury, Harvard University Press
finding: Cited by OpenLearn, Rossner and Cohen & Berryessa as the source for verdict-driven vs evidence-driven deliberation styles and for the deliberation process the story model leaves thin. Not opened.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Citation only. The 1983 reasonable-doubt threshold ratings are reported second-hand in a04.
agent_relevance: Open next as the main empirical base for deliberation processes.

source: Devine, Clayton, Dunford, Seying & Pryce (2001) Jury decision making: 45 years of empirical research on deliberating groups, Psychology, Public Policy, and Law 7(3):622
finding: Named in OpenLearn and in Cohen & Berryessa as the review of deliberating-group evidence. Title and DOI confirmed through Crossref only; the paper was not opened.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Paywalled; unverified details. Do not quote numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Priority for the next pass on the deliberation critique: need its figures for how often final verdict matches the first-ballot majority.

source: Legal Evidence-Authority Dissociation in juror judgment (PMC13719418), citing Carlson & Russo (2001) and Simon & Read (2023)
finding: A recent multistudy paper treats the story model as classic work and pairs it with coherence-based accounts in which evidence and preference reinforce each other, producing shifts before the verdict. This is the usual theoretical move that answers the formalism critique: the story becomes a coherence process.
numbers: No numbers recorded from the model discussion.
limits: Secondary description of other papers; the cited coherence studies were not opened in this run.
agent_relevance: Coherence shifts are a risk for our agent too: evidence that fits the favoured answer gets rated higher after the fact. Rate evidence before the candidate answer is shown.

source: (Dis)passionate law stories: the emotional processes of encoding narratives in court (2022)
finding: Conceptual article on how legal professionals turn court narratives into legal form. It cites the story model and Lempert (1991) for narrative use, and argues that dispassion in court is partly a technique: demarcation, fragmentation and proximation, with doubt and certainty regulating how close the decider gets to the story.
numbers: Conceptual; no empirical numbers.
limits: No experiment; the emotional techniques are proposals.
agent_relevance: A possible reason story form matters: it carries emotion and engagement. For our agent this is a risk to control, not an asset.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror
finding: The authors' own limits statement: the model is a major candidate to explain juror decisions in criminal trials, with many areas still open. Their first four studies used one trial (Commonwealth v. Johnson) or one set of case materials, with student or jury-pool participants and no deliberation measured.
numbers: Chapter covers six studies; samples N=26 (16 analysed), 130, 414, plus recognition and completeness studies.
limits: Single-case foundations; the chapter does not claim deliberation results.
agent_relevance: Treat the founding evidence as about individual construction of an account from one case, which is the scope our scaffold can use.
